vitamin-c.shortDescription: Vitamin C is a water-soluble vitamin and an essential nutrient that the human body cannot produce on its own. It plays a role in collagen formation, the normal function of the immune system, and increasing the absorption of iron from plant-based foods. It is found in a wide variety of vegetables and fruits.
vitamin-c.fullDescription:
When people think of vitamin C, many picture looking after their health during a cold, but vitamin C plays a far more important role in the body than that. It is involved in collagen formation, immune system function and the absorption of iron from food, all of which are processes related to the normal functioning of the body.

Because the human body cannot synthesise vitamin C itself, it must be obtained regularly from food. Common food sources include guava, oranges, kiwi, bell peppers, papaya and broccoli. Getting enough vitamin C from a varied diet is therefore an important foundation of everyday health care.
vitamin-c.howItWorks:
What does vitamin C do?
1. Collagen formation
Vitamin C is required for the function of enzymes involved in collagen formation. Collagen is a key structural protein of the skin, blood vessels, cartilage and connective tissue, so getting enough vitamin C is important for maintaining the normal function of these tissues.
2. Immune system function
Vitamin C plays a role in the function of many types of immune cells and is involved in the body's natural response processes. However, getting enough vitamin C does not mean that taking vitamin C supplements will definitely prevent colds.
3. Protecting cells from oxidative stress
Vitamin C is a water-soluble antioxidant. It plays a role in controlling oxidation reactions that occur in the body and is involved in maintaining cellular balance.
4. Iron absorption
Vitamin C helps increase the absorption of non-heme iron, which is found in plant foods such as beans, grains and leafy green vegetables. Eating foods containing vitamin C together with these foods is therefore one way to help the body absorb iron from a meal more effectively.
Vitamin C and its mechanisms in the body
Vitamin C's main mechanism is acting as an electron donor in biochemical reactions at the cellular level. This property allows vitamin C to contribute to the antioxidant processes that counter free radicals generated naturally by energy metabolism, and helps reduce damage to cell structures caused by oxidative stress.
At the tissue-structure level, vitamin C acts as an essential cofactor for enzymes in the collagen-formation process. Collagen is the main structural protein that helps the skin, blood vessels, cartilage and gums maintain their normal function. Vitamin C also contributes to the normal function of the immune system and helps the body absorb iron from food more effectively.
Because the body cannot store excess vitamin C over the long term, the digestive tract and kidneys regulate vitamin C levels to keep them in balance. Absorption is reduced when high amounts are taken in, and any excess the body does not use is naturally excreted in the urine. This mechanism helps keep the body's vitamin C levels within a range suitable for the normal functioning of its various systems.
vitamin-c.uniqueProperties:
When should you take vitamin C?
For people taking vitamin C as a dietary supplement, it can generally be taken at various times of the day. There is no need to take it only in the morning or before bed, as there is not yet clear evidence that any particular time consistently provides greater benefit.
If vitamin C causes stomach discomfort, taking it with or after a meal may make it easier to tolerate. People who want to increase their absorption of iron from plant sources can choose to eat vitamin C-containing foods together with iron-containing meals.
Food sources of vitamin C
Vitamin C occurs naturally in a wide variety of vegetables and fruits, such as guava, oranges, kiwi, papaya, strawberries, bell peppers and broccoli. The amount of vitamin C may vary depending on the type of food, its freshness and the cooking method.
Because vitamin C is water-soluble and sensitive to heat, prolonged boiling may cause some of it to be lost. Eating fresh, well-washed vegetables and fruits, or choosing cooking methods that use heat only briefly, such as steaming, helps reduce vitamin C losses and supports adequate nutrient intake.
vitamin-c.scientificEvidence:
• Vitamin C is an essential nutrient with scientific evidence supporting its role in many aspects of body function, particularly collagen formation, immune system function and the absorption of iron from plant sources.
• Studies confirm that vitamin C is necessary for collagen formation, which is a key component of the skin, blood vessels and connective tissue. It also acts as an antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative stress.
• As for the immune system, although vitamin C plays a role in immune cell function, the evidence does not clearly support that taking vitamin C supplements can prevent colds in the general population. Getting enough vitamin C is therefore more important than taking high amounts unnecessarily.
This page is provided for information about nutritional roles only. It is not advice for treating or preventing disease.
vitamin-c.safetyInformation:
• The body does not store excess vitamin C, so serious side effects from excessive intake are very rare.
• Intake above 2,000 milligrams per day is not recommended, as it may cause stomach discomfort and diarrhoea.
• High doses may cause kidney stones, although this is uncommon.
• Pregnant women should not take high-dose vitamin C supplements, as this may cause vitamin C deficiency in the baby after birth. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should consult a healthcare professional about the appropriate amount.
keyFunctions: Vitamin C contributes to antioxidant processes
Vitamin C contributes to collagen formation for the normal function of the skin
Vitamin C contributes to the normal function of the immune system
Vitamin C contributes to the protection of cells from free radicals
Vitamin C increases iron absorption

turmeric.shortDescription: Turmeric is a herbal plant with a yellow-orange rhizome that is widely used as a spice in Asian cuisine. It contains active compounds in the curcuminoid group, especially curcumin, which has attracted researchers' interest in relation to inflammatory processes, oxidative stress and the digestive system.
turmeric.fullDescription:
The golden-yellow colour of curries and many other dishes in Thai kitchens comes from a herb we all know well: turmeric. Behind this distinctive colour, however, are natural compounds that have attracted the interest of scientists, especially curcumin, one of the key compounds found in the turmeric rhizome.

Turmeric has the scientific name Curcuma longa L. and belongs to the family Zingiberaceae, the same family as ginger. The part commonly used is the rhizome, an underground stem, not the root as is often thought. The turmeric rhizome contains both natural pigments and essential oils that give it its characteristic aroma and flavour.

The most extensively studied active compounds are the curcuminoids, which consist of curcumin, demethoxycurcumin and bisdemethoxycurcumin. Curcumin has attracted interest in relation to intracellular signalling processes and the response to oxidative stress.
turmeric.howItWorks:
Turmeric and its mechanisms in the body
1. Relationship to the body's inflammatory processes
Curcumin has been studied in relation to intracellular signalling pathways such as NF-κB, which is involved in regulating signalling molecules in inflammatory processes.
2. Role in the response to oxidative stress
Curcuminoids have a chemical structure associated with antioxidant properties. They have been studied in relation to the function of the cell's defence systems against oxidative stress, including the Nrf2 pathway, which is involved in regulating certain enzymes in the body.
3. Relationship to the digestive system
Turmeric has a history of use in herbal formulas related to the digestive tract, and curcumin has been studied in relation to the response of the gastrointestinal lining and the signalling processes associated with stomach discomfort.
turmeric.uniqueProperties:
Forms and consumption of turmeric
Turmeric is a herb and spice that has long been bound up with ways of life and cooking. It is consumed in the following forms:
• Fresh turmeric rhizome: the fresh rhizome is pounded, crushed or juiced for use as a main ingredient in curry pastes and southern Thai dishes, or to add natural colour and aroma to food.
• Dried turmeric powder: the turmeric rhizome is sliced, dried and ground into a fine powder for use as a cooking spice, mixed with warm water as a drink, or filled into capsules for consumption.
• Turmeric extract: turmeric undergoes an extraction process to control the curcuminoid content at a consistent concentration. It is commonly filled into dietary supplements in capsule or tablet form.
turmeric.scientificEvidence:
1. Studies on the digestive system
A randomised controlled trial by Kongkam et al. (2023) studied the use of curcumin in people with functional dyspepsia, comparing it with the drug omeprazole and with the two used together.
The study found that participants' dyspepsia symptom scores improved in each group, and no significant difference between groups was found in the main outcomes assessed. However, this study did not have a placebo group, so it cannot be concluded that curcumin is more effective than using no active substance.
In addition, the trial results come from the use of curcumin in a specified amount and form; they are not evidence that general consumption of turmeric can treat indigestion.
2. Studies on joint discomfort
A meta-analysis by Daily et al. (2016) pooled randomised trials of turmeric extract and curcumin in people with joint symptoms and found that some studies reported improved joint discomfort scores and joint function.
However, the studies differed in the type of extract, dose, duration of use and study quality, so larger trials with more consistent standards are still needed.
3. Studies on oxidative stress and inflammatory processes
Curcumin has attracted researchers' interest in relation to biomarkers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and substances associated with the body's inflammatory processes.
Some studies have reported changes in these markers after taking curcumin extract, but the trial results are not entirely consistent, and changes in laboratory markers do not necessarily mean there will be clear long-term health benefits.
4. Studies on curcumin absorption
A study by Shoba et al. (1998) examined the use of curcumin together with piperine, the key compound in black pepper, and found that using them together in a specified amount increased the amount of curcumin detected in the body compared with curcumin alone.
However, increased absorption does not confirm increased health effectiveness, and piperine may also affect the metabolism or levels of certain drugs in the body.
This information is provided for education about turmeric. It is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating disease.
turmeric.safetyInformation:
• Concentrated turmeric extract may cause stomach discomfort, nausea, diarrhoea or acid reflux in some people.
• People with liver disease or a history of liver abnormalities should consult a doctor before using concentrated extracts.
• People with gallstones or bile duct abnormalities should consult a doctor before use, as turmeric may affect gallbladder function.
• People taking anticoagulants, antiplatelet drugs or other regular medications should consult a doctor or pharmacist before use.
• Pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid using concentrated extracts in amounts higher than those normally found in food.
• If you develop yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine or unusual fatigue while using the product, stop using it and see a doctor.
keyFunctions: Contains curcuminoids, which have been studied in relation to the inflammatory response
Has been clinically studied in relation to stomach comfort and certain digestive symptoms
Has been researched in relation to measures of joint discomfort and mobility

bilberry.nameTh: บิลเบอร์รี่
bilberry.shortDescription: Bilberry is a fruit of the berry family containing active compounds in the anthocyanin group, which has led researchers to take an interest in bilberry in relation to eye health, blood vessel function and the response to oxidative stress.
bilberry.fullDescription:
Bilberry may look similar to the blueberry that many people know, but cutting the fruit open reveals an interesting difference: the inner flesh of the bilberry is usually a deep reddish-purple, unlike many cultivated blueberry varieties, which have pale flesh. These colours are not there merely to make the fruit attractive; they come from natural compounds called anthocyanins, which have attracted considerable interest in health research.

Bilberry has the scientific name Vaccinium myrtillus L. and belongs to the family Ericaceae. It grows naturally in forests and temperate zones of Europe and parts of Asia. Although it belongs to the same genus as the blueberry, it is not the same species.

The anthocyanins in bilberry comprise many different compounds. They are a group of natural pigments whose chemical properties are associated with antioxidant activity, so researchers have taken an interest in the role of these compounds in cell and blood vessel function, as well as in matters related to eye health.
bilberry.howItWorks:
Bilberry and its mechanisms in the body
1. The role of anthocyanins in oxidative stress
Anthocyanins are natural pigments in bilberry with antioxidant properties. They can interact with free radicals and with chemical processes associated with oxidative stress.
2. Relationship to eye cell function
Anthocyanins from bilberry have been studied in relation to intracellular signalling processes and the response to cellular stress in the eye.
3. Relationship to blood vessel function
The polyphenols in bilberry have been studied in relation to the function of the blood vessel wall, which helps regulate the dilation and constriction of blood vessels, as well as the response to signalling molecules in the body.
bilberry.uniqueProperties:
Forms and consumption of bilberry
Bilberry is a fruit of the berry family that is dark blue to purplish-black in both its skin and flesh. Because the fresh fruit is delicate and bruises and spoils easily, it is commonly processed for consumption in the following forms:
• Frozen bilberries and dried fruit: the fresh fruit is quick-frozen or dried for use as an ingredient in cereals and yoghurt, or made into jams and desserts.
• Bilberry juice and herbal tea: the fresh fruit is pressed into ready-to-drink juice, or the dried fruit and leaves are ground for brewing as tea.
• Bilberry extract: bilberries undergo an extraction process to control the anthocyanin content at a consistent concentration. It is commonly filled into dietary supplements in capsule form for convenient intake and a defined amount of the active compounds.
bilberry.scientificEvidence:
1. Studies on eye fatigue
Ozawa et al. (2015) studied people who work with computer screens, using bilberry extract at 480 milligrams per day for 8 weeks. They found that some measures of eye fatigue and symptoms reported by participants improved compared with the placebo group.
However, 80 participants completed the trial, and positive results were not seen for every type of measure, so it cannot yet be concluded that bilberry extract helps reduce eye fatigue in everyone.
2. Studies on the function of the muscles used to adjust focus
A randomised, placebo-controlled trial in 109 adults studied intake of a standardised bilberry extract at 240 milligrams per day for 12 weeks and found significant differences in some measures related to the function of the focusing muscles after using the eyes on screens.
Although the results are interesting, the study examined specific measures; it is not evidence that bilberry can correct short-sightedness or long-sightedness, or improve sharpness of vision in general.
3. Studies on vision in the dark
A systematic review by Canter and Ernst (2004) assessed placebo-controlled trials of anthocyanosides from bilberry and found that most methodologically rigorous trials did not support the claim that bilberry improves night vision in people with normal eyesight.
There is therefore not yet sufficient reliable evidence to claim that bilberry helps people see better at night.
4. Studies on blood vessels and oxidative stress
Anthocyanins and polyphenols from bilberry have been studied in relation to blood vessel function and biomarkers associated with oxidative stress, but human trial results still vary depending on the type of extract, dose and participant group.
It therefore cannot yet be confirmed that taking bilberry helps prevent vascular disease or improves blood circulation to a clinically significant degree.
This information is provided for education about bilberry. It is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating disease.
bilberry.safetyInformation:
• Eating bilberries in amounts normally found in food is generally considered safe.
• People taking regular medications, especially those related to blood clotting, should consult a doctor or pharmacist before using concentrated extracts.
• Pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid using bilberry extract in amounts higher than those found in food, as safety data are still insufficient.
keyFunctions: Contains anthocyanins, which contribute to antioxidant activity and eye cell function
Has been researched in relation to blood vessel function and blood circulation
Contains polyphenols that have been studied in relation to the response to oxidative stress

black-pepper.shortDescription: Black pepper contains piperine, the key component responsible for its characteristic pungent heat. Beyond its culinary use, piperine has also attracted interest in studies on the absorption and metabolism of certain substances in the body.
black-pepper.fullDescription:
Black pepper may seem like just a spice that many people use to add flavour to food, but in scientific circles the active compounds hidden in peppercorns have attracted more interest than their heat, especially piperine, which has been studied for its ability to alter the body's absorption and handling of certain substances.

Black pepper has the scientific name Piper nigrum L. and belongs to the family Piperaceae. The black pepper used as a spice comes from fruit harvested before it is fully ripe and then dried, which gives the skin its dark, wrinkled appearance. This differs from white pepper, which undergoes a process to remove the outer skin layer.

The highlight of black pepper is piperine, an alkaloid that contributes to its pungency and has been studied as a substance that may affect the bioavailability of certain compounds. A widely noted example is the study of piperine used together with curcumin from turmeric.
black-pepper.howItWorks:
Black pepper and its mechanisms in the body
1. Absorption of bioactive compounds
Piperine has been studied in relation to changes in the amount of certain substances that enter the bloodstream after ingestion. It may affect absorption, transport of substances and their metabolism in the digestive tract or related organs.
2. Function of enzymes and transport proteins
Laboratory studies have found that piperine can interact with certain enzymes and transport proteins involved in the body's handling of substances, such as the CYP enzyme system and the transport protein P-glycoprotein.
3. Perception of pungency
Piperine is associated with the activation of certain sensory receptors, such as TRPV1, which is involved in perceiving heat and irritation. The pungency of black pepper therefore has a different chemical basis from capsaicin found in chilli peppers, even though they share some of the same sensory receptors.
black-pepper.uniqueProperties:
Forms and consumption of black pepper
Black pepper is a spice used widely around the world, and it is processed for consumption in forms ranging from household use to the dietary supplement industry, as follows:
• Whole and ground black peppercorns: dried whole peppercorns, or peppercorns ground finely or coarsely, are used as a main cooking spice, providing pungent heat and a characteristic aroma from natural essential oils.
• Black pepper extract: black peppercorns undergo an extraction process to control the content of the active compound piperine at a standardised, consistent concentration. It is commonly filled into dietary supplements in capsule form, or used together with other nutrients to support the body's absorption.
• Black pepper oleoresin: extracted with solvents to draw out both the pungency and the concentrated aroma in the form of a viscous liquid. It is commonly used in the food-processing industry to flavour products to a consistent standard.
black-pepper.scientificEvidence:
1. Studies on piperine used with curcumin in humans
A study by Shoba et al. examined curcumin used together with piperine in healthy volunteers and found that giving 20 milligrams of piperine together with 2 grams of curcumin greatly increased the bioavailability of curcumin compared with curcumin alone.
However, this study had a small number of participants, used specific amounts of the substances and measured blood levels of curcumin. It did not prove that increased absorption leads to greater health benefits, or that the same results apply to every product formulation.
2. Evidence on the absorption of other substances
A study by Badmaev et al. (1999) examined piperine used together with beta-carotene in humans and found differences in blood beta-carotene levels between the group that also received piperine and the comparison group.
The results support the possibility that piperine may alter the bioavailability of certain substances, but they are not sufficient to conclude that piperine increases the absorption of all vitamins, minerals or nutrients.
3. Evidence on the digestive system and overall health
Although black pepper has a long history of use as a spice, clinical research in humans directly assessing the effects of black pepper extract on digestive function is still limited.
Much of the data on antioxidant activity and inflammatory processes comes from cell or animal studies, so it should not be used to confirm that black pepper can prevent or treat gastrointestinal disorders in humans.
This information is provided for education about black pepper. It is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating disease.
black-pepper.safetyInformation:
• Consuming large amounts of black pepper or its extract may cause gastrointestinal irritation or stomach discomfort in some people.
• Piperine may alter the absorption and elimination of certain drugs, so consult a doctor or pharmacist before using products containing concentrated piperine together with regular medications.
• People with underlying conditions or who take drugs whose levels must be closely controlled should take particular care.
• Pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid using concentrated piperine extracts without advice from a healthcare professional, as safety data are still limited.
keyFunctions: Contains piperine, a key alkaloid that gives its characteristic pungent heat
Has been studied in relation to altering the bioavailability of certain substances
Is associated with the absorption and metabolism of substances in the body
Contains antioxidants in laboratory studies

cordyceps.shortDescription: Cordyceps is a name used for several species of fungi with a history of use in Asian herbal formulas, especially Tibetan cordyceps and golden cordyceps. They contain active compounds of interest such as cordycepin, adenosine and polysaccharides, and are currently being studied in relation to cellular energy production and physical performance.
cordyceps.fullDescription:
Cordyceps is a herb with a story unlike that of ordinary plants, because cordyceps is in fact a fungus, not a root or a herbal plant. Some species of cordyceps grow naturally on insect larvae, while others can be cultivated in controlled environments.

What makes cordyceps interesting is its many groups of natural compounds, especially cordycepin, which is found prominently in golden cordyceps, as well as adenosine and polysaccharides, which have been studied in relation to cell function and energy metabolism. Cordyceps is also currently attracting interest in research on exercise endurance.
cordyceps.howItWorks:
Cordyceps and its mechanisms in the body
1. Relationship to cellular energy production
Cordyceps contains certain compounds that have been studied in relation to cellular pathways such as AMPK, which is involved in regulating the body's energy balance, particularly when cells need to adjust energy use and production to suit different conditions.
2. The role of cordycepin in cell function
Cordycepin, or 3'-deoxyadenosine, is a compound with a structure similar to adenosine, a substance involved in many cellular processes. Researchers are studying whether cordycepin may interact with certain signalling pathways associated with the cellular stress response.
3. Immune system response
Polysaccharides from certain fungi have been studied in relation to their interaction with immune cells and changes in signalling molecules associated with the body's responses.
cordyceps.uniqueProperties:
Forms and consumption of cordyceps
Cordyceps is an ancient Chinese herb that today is commonly cultivated in closed systems for safety and freedom from contaminants. It is processed for consumption in the following forms:
• Dried cordyceps: whole cultivated cordyceps fruiting bodies that have been dried can be used to make soup, braised with meat, or brewed as a herbal tea according to traditional Chinese medicine formulas, to enjoy their natural flavour and nutrients.
• Finely ground cordyceps powder: dried cordyceps fruiting bodies are ground into a powder for brewing as a drink or filling into capsules for easy consumption.
• Standardised cordyceps extract: cordyceps undergoes an extraction process to achieve a higher concentration, with the key active compounds such as cordycepin and adenosine controlled at standardised levels. It is commonly filled into dietary supplements in capsule form.
cordyceps.scientificEvidence:
1. Studies on exercise endurance
A study by Hirsch et al. (2017) examined a product containing Cordyceps militaris together with other mushrooms in healthy adults, assessing measures of endurance and high-intensity exercise.
Some of the results showed changes in measures of physical performance. However, because the product contained multiple ingredients, it cannot be concluded that all of the effects were due to cordyceps alone, and the number of participants was also limited.
2. Studies on cordyceps use in older adults
A study by Chen et al. (2010) examined a product derived from cultivated Cordyceps sinensis in healthy older adults and found changes in some measures related to exercise performance.
However, the product used in the trial had specific characteristics, and the results do not show that cordyceps can increase strength or physical performance in all population groups.
3. Evidence on cordycepin and cell function
Cordycepin is a compound of interest in laboratory research and has been studied in relation to the regulation of cell function and many biological response processes.
However, most of the evidence is still at the level of cell or animal experiments, so these data are not sufficient to confirm that taking cordyceps extract containing cordycepin will produce the same results in humans.
This information is provided for education about cordyceps. It is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating disease.
cordyceps.safetyInformation:
• Each species of cordyceps may have a different chemical composition and safety profile, so check the scientific name and source of the raw material.
• Some users may experience stomach discomfort, nausea, diarrhoea or allergic reactions.
• People taking anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs should consult a doctor before use, as there are concerns about herb-drug interactions.
• People taking immunosuppressants or who have immune system disorders should consult a doctor before use.
• Pregnant women, breastfeeding women and children should avoid using cordyceps extract without advice from a healthcare professional, as safety data are still insufficient.
keyFunctions: Rich in natural compounds such as cordycepin, adenosine and polysaccharides, with amounts varying by species
Has been studied in relation to energy metabolism and cell function
Has some clinical studies on physical performance and exercise endurance
Contains compounds that have been studied in relation to the immune response at the laboratory level

vitamin-b12.shortDescription: Vitamin B12 is a water-soluble vitamin that plays an important role in nervous system function, red blood cell formation and DNA synthesis. It is found naturally in animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs and dairy products. Although the body needs only a small amount, an adequate intake is necessary for its various processes to function normally.
vitamin-b12.fullDescription:
Vitamin B12, or cobalamin, is a water-soluble vitamin that contains the mineral cobalt. It is found naturally in animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs and dairy products. Unlike many other B vitamins, vitamin B12 can be stored in the liver for long periods, so it may take several years before a deficiency produces clear symptoms.

The key functions of vitamin B12 are its involvement in red blood cell formation and DNA synthesis, which is necessary for cell division. It is also involved in forming and maintaining the myelin sheath that surrounds nerve fibres, helping the nervous system transmit signals normally, and plays a role in nutrient metabolism so that the body can make use of nutrients.

However, getting vitamin B12 from food does not mean the body will absorb it fully, because this vitamin relies on stomach acid and a protein called intrinsic factor to be absorbed in the small intestine. Older adults, people who eat mainly plant-based diets and people with nutrient absorption problems may therefore be at risk of insufficient vitamin B12 intake, even if some of them eat normally.
vitamin-b12.howItWorks:
Vitamin B12 and its mechanisms in the body
1. The nervous system and nerve signalling
Vitamin B12 is important for forming and protecting the myelin sheath, a fatty layer that surrounds nerve fibres and helps nerve signals travel efficiently. Having enough vitamin B12 is therefore part of maintaining normal nervous system function.
2. The blood system and cell formation
Vitamin B12 works together with folate in DNA synthesis, which is necessary for cell division and development, especially of red blood cell precursors in the bone marrow. If the body lacks vitamin B12, red blood cell formation may become abnormal.
3. Metabolism and energy use
Vitamin B12 acts as a coenzyme in the metabolism of certain nutrients, helping the body convert substrates for use in cellular energy production.
vitamin-b12.uniqueProperties:
Food sources of vitamin B12
• Meat and organ meats, such as beef, beef liver and chicken liver
• Fish and seafood, such as salmon, tuna, shellfish and certain other seafood
• Eggs and dairy products, such as chicken eggs, milk, yoghurt and cheese
• Foods fortified with vitamin B12, such as some cereals, some plant-based milk formulations and nutritional yeast with added vitamin B12
• Dietary supplements, such as B-complex vitamins, multivitamins and dedicated vitamin B12 products
vitamin-b12.scientificEvidence:
1. Vitamin B12 and nervous system function and memory
A 2021 systematic review pooled 16 randomised trials with a total of 6,276 participants to assess the effects of supplementing vitamin B12 alone or together with other B vitamins. It found no clear evidence that such supplementation improves thinking and memory function in people without a clear vitamin B12 deficiency or severe neurological disorders.
2. Vitamin B12 and red blood cell formation
Clinical information from the NIH explains that vitamin B12 is necessary for DNA synthesis and normal red blood cell formation. Vitamin B12 deficiency may cause abnormal red blood cell formation, including megaloblastic anaemia, which reflects the importance of this vitamin to the blood system.
3. Vitamin B12, fatigue and energy metabolism
Although vitamin B12 plays a role in energy metabolism, clinical studies have not yet found sufficient evidence that vitamin B12 supplementation reduces fatigue in people who are not deficient. A 2021 analysis found only one eligible study on fatigue, so no conclusion can yet be drawn about its effectiveness.
This information is provided for education about vitamin B12. It is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating disease.
vitamin-b12.safetyInformation:
• People who eat mainly vegetarian or vegan diets, older adults and people with nutrient absorption problems may be at risk of insufficient vitamin B12 intake.
• Certain drugs, such as metformin and antacids in the proton pump inhibitor group, may affect the absorption or levels of vitamin B12 when used for a long time.
• People who experience numbness or tingling in the hands and feet, unusual fatigue, or suspect a vitamin B12 deficiency should consult a doctor to assess the cause. Vitamins should not be taken as a substitute for diagnostic testing.
keyFunctions: Vitamin B12 helps produce substances needed for red blood cell formation
Vitamin B12 contributes to the normal function of the nervous system and brain
Vitamin B12 contributes to normal energy-yielding metabolism
Vitamin B12 contributes to the normal function of the immune system

vitamin-d3.shortDescription: Vitamin D3 plays an important role in the absorption of calcium and phosphorus to maintain normal bones and teeth. It is also involved in muscle and immune system function, and the body can produce it when the skin receives enough UVB radiation from sunlight.
vitamin-d3.fullDescription:
Vitamin D3, or cholecalciferol, is a fat-soluble vitamin that the body can produce itself when the skin is exposed to UVB radiation from sunlight. This does not mean, however, that everyone gets enough, especially older adults, people who spend most of their time indoors and people with limited fat absorption.

Vitamin D3 can also be obtained from certain foods, such as salmon, mackerel, egg yolks and vitamin D-fortified foods. Vitamin D3 is converted in the liver and kidneys into a form the body can use to regulate various processes.

Vitamin D3 plays an important role in helping absorb calcium and phosphorus from the intestine. These minerals are essential for building and maintaining strong bones and teeth. Vitamin D3 also contributes to normal muscle function and is involved in regulating the response of immune cells, making it a nutrient that is important to many body systems, not just bone health.
vitamin-d3.howItWorks:
Vitamin D3 and its mechanisms in the body
1. The skeletal system and mineral absorption
Vitamin D3 helps regulate the absorption of calcium and phosphorus in the small intestine so that the body has enough minerals for the continuous process of building and remodelling bone. It therefore works together with calcium to maintain normal bones and teeth.
2. The muscular system and movement
Vitamin D is involved in muscle function and in regulating calcium balance, a mineral that is essential for muscle contraction. Having enough vitamin D is therefore one component of maintaining normal muscle function.
3. The immune system and cell function
Many types of immune cells have vitamin D receptors, which are involved in regulating the immune system's responses. Vitamin D therefore plays a role in the normal function of this system.
vitamin-d3.uniqueProperties:
Sources of vitamin D3
• Sunlight: the skin can produce vitamin D3 when exposed to UVB radiation, but you should not stay in strong sunlight for long periods to increase vitamin D, because UV radiation increases the risk of skin damage.
• Natural foods: such as salmon, mackerel, fish liver oil and egg yolks.
• Vitamin D-fortified foods: such as milk and certain food products with added vitamin D3.
• Dietary supplements: available as capsules, tablets and drops, including formulas combined with calcium or other nutrients.
vitamin-d3.scientificEvidence:
1. Vitamin D3 and maintaining blood vitamin D levels
Studies comparing vitamins D2 and D3 have found that D3 can generally raise blood levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D, or 25(OH)D, more and maintain those levels for longer across many study designs. This is one of the reasons vitamin D3 is widely used in dietary supplements.
2. Vitamin D3 and bone strength
The VITAL trial in more than 25,000 adults studied supplementation with 2,000 IU of vitamin D3 per day and found that it did not significantly reduce the risk of fractures compared with placebo in adults, most of whom already had sufficient vitamin D levels.
These results help make clear that vitamin D is necessary for bones, but additional supplementation does not mean it will provide extra benefit for everyone.
3. Vitamin D3 and muscle function
Vitamin D is important for muscle function, and vitamin D deficiency may be associated with muscle weakness. However, clinical trials studying vitamin D supplementation for muscle strength and performance have produced inconsistent results, so it should not be claimed that vitamin D3 supplementation increases muscle strength in general.
This information is provided for education about vitamin D3. It is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating disease.
vitamin-d3.safetyInformation:
• Vitamin D3 is a fat-soluble vitamin, so it can accumulate in the body if more is taken than needed.
• Taking high doses of vitamin D3 for a long time may raise blood calcium levels and harm the kidneys or other body systems.
• People with kidney disease, high blood calcium or who are taking certain medications should consult a doctor before taking vitamin D3 supplements.
keyFunctions: Helps the absorption and utilisation of calcium and phosphorus
Contributes to the maintenance of normal bones and teeth
Plays a role in normal muscle function
Is involved in the normal function of the immune system
Is involved in cell division and cell function
Contributes to maintaining balanced blood calcium levels

l-cysteine.nameTh: แอล-ซิสเทอีน
l-cysteine.shortDescription: L-Cysteine is an amino acid that plays an important role in protein synthesis, especially of keratin, a component of hair and nails. It is also one of the precursors the body uses to produce glutathione, a substance involved in the cell's antioxidant system.
l-cysteine.fullDescription:
L-Cysteine is a sulphur-containing amino acid and is classified as an amino acid that the body can synthesise under normal conditions, through the conversion of the amino acid methionine via various intermediates.

What makes L-cysteine interesting is that it has two distinct important roles: it is a component of the protein keratin, which is involved in the structure of hair and nails, and it is a precursor for producing glutathione, which is part of the cell's system for regulating free-radical balance.

Because of these properties, L-cysteine has attracted considerable interest in biochemistry, protein structure and the study of substances related to the health of the skin, hair and nails.
l-cysteine.howItWorks:
L-Cysteine and its mechanisms in the body
When the body receives protein from food, the digestive system breaks it down into amino acids and small peptides before they are absorbed and used in various processes, including the production of proteins and compounds necessary for cells. L-Cysteine therefore plays an important role through two main processes, as follows:
1. Glutathione production
Glutathione is a compound made from three amino acids: glutamate, cysteine and glycine. Cysteine is often one of the factors that affects the rate of glutathione synthesis in cells. Glutathione takes part in the system that regulates oxidative balance and in many biochemical processes.
2. Forming and maintaining the structure of keratin
Keratin is a key protein found in hair, nails and skin. The amino acid cysteine can form disulphide bonds between protein chains, which stabilise the keratin structure. These bonds are all involved in the strength and physical characteristics of hair and nails.
l-cysteine.uniqueProperties:
Food sources of L-cysteine
• Meat and poultry, such as chicken, pork and beef
• Fish and seafood, such as salmon, tuna and shrimp
• Eggs, such as chicken eggs and duck eggs
• Milk and dairy products, such as milk, yoghurt and cheese
• Beans and legumes, such as soybeans, peanuts and lentils
• Seeds, such as sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds and sesame
• Grains, such as oats, wheat and whole grains
l-cysteine.scientificEvidence:
1. Evidence on antioxidant activity
Biochemical studies show that the amount of cysteine available to cells is associated with glutathione synthesis. However, clinical evidence confirming that taking L-cysteine alone can raise glutathione levels or affect long-term health is still limited.
2. Studies on hair and nail health
Research on protein structure supports the role of cysteine in the properties of keratin, but clinical studies on taking L-cysteine to strengthen hair, reduce hair loss or directly care for nails are not yet sufficient to draw clear conclusions about its effectiveness.
3. Evidence on skin and skin pigmentation
Glutathione and substances related to skin pigment formation have been studied, but the results of these studies cannot be used to directly confirm the effectiveness of L-cysteine, because of differences in the substances studied, the way they were used and the outcomes measured.
This page is provided for information about the composition and scientific study of L-cysteine. It is not advice for treating or preventing disease.
l-cysteine.safetyInformation:
• People with amino acid metabolism disorders, and pregnant and breastfeeding women, should get advice from a doctor before use, as there may be individual limitations.
• For high-dose intake, do not increase the amount on your own, as data on the safety of continuous high-dose use are still insufficient.
• When using it for skin, hair and nail care, do not expect specific results from taking L-cysteine without supporting clinical evidence.
keyFunctions: A key precursor in the synthesis of glutathione, which plays a role in the cell's antioxidant system
Is a component of the protein keratin found in hair, nails and skin
Contributes to maintaining protein structure through the formation of disulphide bonds
Plays a role in maintaining oxidative balance within cells
Takes part in the body's metabolism of amino acids and sulphur compounds

l-arginine.nameTh: แอล-อาร์จินีน
l-arginine.shortDescription: L-Arginine is an amino acid that plays a role in protein synthesis and in the production of nitric oxide, a signalling molecule involved in blood vessel function. It also takes part in the removal of ammonia and the synthesis of important compounds in the body.
l-arginine.fullDescription:
The human circulatory system relies on the heart, blood vessels and many signalling substances working together. One substance that plays an important role is nitric oxide, which is involved in regulating the constriction and relaxation of blood vessels. L-Arginine is an amino acid that the body uses as a precursor to produce nitric oxide through biochemical processes.

In addition to its role in nitric oxide production, L-arginine takes part in the urea cycle, which helps the body convert ammonia into urea for excretion in the urine. It is also a precursor in the synthesis of creatine, which is involved in the cell's energy system.

The body can synthesise L-arginine itself under normal conditions, but at certain times when demand increases, such as during growth or severe illness, the body's own production may not meet its needs. L-Arginine can also be obtained from protein-containing foods such as meat, fish, beans and seeds.
l-arginine.howItWorks:
L-Arginine and its mechanisms in the body
1. Nitric oxide production and blood vessel function
In the body, the enzyme nitric oxide synthase (NOS) can convert L-arginine into nitric oxide, which acts as a signalling molecule involved in relaxing the smooth muscle of the blood vessel wall. This process plays an important part in the natural regulation of blood vessel diameter and blood flow.
2. Ammonia removal through the urea cycle
When the body metabolises amino acids, ammonia is produced, which must be converted into a form that can be excreted. L-Arginine is a key intermediate in the urea cycle. This process takes place mainly in the liver, before urea is excreted by the kidneys.
3. Creatine synthesis and cell function
L-Arginine takes part in the synthesis of creatine together with other amino acids. Creatine is a substance involved in storing and transferring energy within cells, especially muscle cells.
l-arginine.uniqueProperties:
Food sources of L-arginine
• Meat, such as chicken, pork and beef
• Fish and seafood
• Soybeans and soy products
• Nuts, such as almonds and walnuts
• Seeds, such as pumpkin seeds and sesame seeds
• Milk and dairy products
l-arginine.scientificEvidence:
• The production of nitric oxide from L-arginine is a physiological process that has been clearly studied.
• Some research has found that L-arginine supplementation may affect blood pressure levels in certain groups, but results vary depending on health status and study design.
• Evidence from studies on physical performance is still limited, and overall no consistent benefit from L-arginine supplementation has been found.
• Some trials in healthy adults did not find that L-arginine supplementation significantly increased nitric oxide markers or muscle strength.
This page is provided for information about nutritional roles only. It is not advice for treating or preventing disease.
l-arginine.safetyInformation:
• May cause nausea, abdominal pain, bloating or diarrhoea in some people.
• People taking blood pressure-lowering medications should consult a doctor before taking it, as low blood pressure may occur.
• People taking nitroglycerin or medications for erectile dysfunction, such as sildenafil, should consult a doctor before use.
• People taking anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs should be cautious about using it together with them.
• People who have recently had a heart attack should not use L-arginine supplements without advice from a doctor.
• People with asthma or a history of allergies should be cautious, as it may worsen symptoms in some cases.
keyFunctions: An amino acid that the body uses for protein synthesis
A precursor in the production of nitric oxide, which is involved in blood vessel relaxation
Takes part in the urea cycle, the process that removes ammonia from the body
Is involved in the synthesis of creatine, which plays a role in the cell's energy system

siberian-ginseng.nameTh: โสมไซบีเรีย
siberian-ginseng.shortDescription: Siberian ginseng is a herbal plant that is distinct from common ginseng, with active compounds in the eleutheroside group found in its roots and rhizomes. It is one of the plants that has attracted interest in studies on fatigue, physical endurance and the stress response.
siberian-ginseng.fullDescription:
Siberian ginseng, with the scientific name Eleutherococcus senticosus, is a herbal plant in the family Araliaceae that has attracted interest in studies on fatigue, physical endurance and the stress response, particularly in the context of the adaptogen concept, which concerns the study of natural substances that may play a role in the body's adaptation processes when facing stress.

The parts commonly used as raw material are the roots and rhizomes, which contain many compounds, especially eleutheroside B and eleutheroside E, which are used as markers in quality testing of certain types of extract. Siberian ginseng differs from Korean ginseng (Panax ginseng) in both its botanical classification and its chemical composition, so data on the effectiveness of the two cannot be used interchangeably.
siberian-ginseng.howItWorks:
Siberian ginseng and its mechanisms in the body
Siberian ginseng is a plant that has attracted interest in studies of the body's response to stress and fatigue, especially the compounds in the eleutheroside group, whose biological activity has been studied at the cellular level and in laboratory animals.
Some research focuses on the relationship of these compounds to the stress-response system, cell function and processes associated with oxidative stress, a condition caused by an imbalance between free radicals and the body's defence systems.
siberian-ginseng.uniqueProperties:
Forms and consumption of Siberian ginseng
Because the fresh root is hard, pungent and leaves a bitter taste on the tongue, it is commonly processed and extracted to draw out its active compounds for use, as follows:
• Herbal tea: the dried root is ground or chopped into small pieces for brewing with hot water.
• Liquid extract: extracted with alcohol or water to draw out the eleutherosides.
• Dietary supplements: in capsule or tablet form, which is the most popular form and allows the most precise control of the amount of active compounds.
siberian-ginseng.scientificEvidence:
• Fatigue and weakness: the EMA accepts the use of Siberian ginseng root in traditional herbal medicine for symptoms of fatigue and weakness, based on its long history of use, not on evidence of effectiveness from clinical trials.
• Physical endurance: there have been studies on physical performance and fatigue, but the results are still inconsistent and not sufficient to confirm that it helps increase endurance in the general population.
• Immune system: the biological activity of compounds in Siberian ginseng has been studied, but there is still a lack of clinical evidence of sufficient quality to confirm immune benefits in humans.
This page is provided for information about nutritional roles only. It is not advice for treating or preventing disease.
siberian-ginseng.safetyInformation:
• People with heart disease or abnormal blood pressure should consult a doctor before taking it.
• People taking medications for chronic conditions, especially digoxin, should consult a doctor or pharmacist before use.
• Insomnia, irritability, headache or a rapid heartbeat may occur in some people.
keyFunctions: Has been scientifically studied in relation to fatigue and weakness
Has attracted interest in studies of the body's response to stress
Has been researched in relation to endurance and physical performance
Has compounds that have been studied in relation to oxidative stress
